overview: Ahé is the self-name of the Karipuna of Rondônia, a Tupi-Kawahib people associated with Brazil’s Jacy-Paraná and Mutum-Paraná rivers. They are distinct from the Karipuna of Amapá.

periods.title: Intensified contact and severe losses
periods.summary: A Funai contact team operated from Panorama in 1976. Frequent visits and relocation near the post were followed by devastating epidemics. This period transformed community life without ending the people’s existence.

periods.title: A recognized territory under pressure
periods.summary: The Karipuna Indigenous Territory was ratified in 1998. Recognition did not eliminate incursions or the community’s need to defend its land.

periods.title: Territorial defence and public testimony
periods.summary: Karipuna advocacy was combined with overflight and satellite evidence of forest destruction. Public testimony and collective organization brought threats to wider attention.

items.text: In his 2022 oral-history interview, Adriano Karipuna recalls learning to make arrows and catching fish with them as a child. His mother roasted the catch and kept it in banana or babassu leaves for the next day. The recollection connects skilled fishing, household food preparation and avoiding waste.

Adriano also remembers a palm-thatched house near the river. He describes the roof’s cool interior alongside its need for regular replacement as insects weakened the material and rain entered. This is a particular household’s experience of building and maintenance, rather than a claim that every Karipuna house was identical.

Forest loss affects more than the availability of food. In the same interview, Adriano explains that clearing and burning destroyed places supplying material for bows and arrows. He still fished with surviving arrows, while making new ones had become difficult. Environmental damage therefore interrupted the practice of a learned craft.

In his 2017 account, Adriano describes fishing, cassava flour, Brazil nuts and açaí as sources of subsistence and income. Produce was sold to buyers in town. The combination shows that forest and river livelihoods could support exchange with urban markets while remaining important to life in the village.

Studying in town brought transport costs, living expenses and racist treatment from classmates, Adriano reports. He described education as a way to gain skills useful to his people. His account makes the journey between village and city part of community history, rather than treating urban residence as the loss of Indigenous identity.

A 2023 field study at Panorama records garden plots and a flour-processing house, with flour used at home and sold in Porto Velho. These working spaces connect cultivation, processing and income. The report also identifies difficulties transporting and packaging produce for sale.

The field study records an Indigenous teacher passing the language to children. Community concerns included aligning school activities with the Brazil-nut harvest. This joins classroom learning with seasonal work, rather than assuming that education happens only inside a school building.

sections.title: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity

items.text: Funai reports from the 1970s describe visits between the contact post and large communal houses on the Contra and Mutum-Paraná waterways. ISA’s historical account contrasts official descriptions of successful contact with the illnesses and deaths that followed. Administrative records need to be read alongside their consequences for families.

The 2023 study combined interviews, field notes and questionnaires with community members and health workers. Its findings are a dated account of conditions and priorities, not a timeless description of Karipuna culture or a current census of everyone belonging to the people.

Greenpeace’s account of its work in 2019 describes combining aerial observations and satellite images with Karipuna reports of invasion. These different forms of evidence made forest clearing visible beyond the territory. They document particular monitoring efforts; a short-term change in clearing does not establish lasting protection.

Karipuna leaders also spoke in international forums and built solidarity with other Indigenous peoples. These public interventions carried community demands beyond Rondônia. Protecting land, communicating its significance and insisting on continued existence are achievements in political organization as well as responses to danger.

ending.text: The Karipuna continue as a living people. Recent fieldwork documents food production, language teaching and collective demands, despite invasion and barriers to services. Their recognized territory and continuing community life cannot be reduced to the map’s 1492 to 1500 interval.
